title: Sales Analysis III
statement:
Two tables record a shop's products and their sales:

- `Product(product_id, product_name, unit_price)`: one row per product; `product_id` is unique.
- `Sales(seller_id, product_id, buyer_id, sale_date, quantity, price)`: one row per sale. Rows may repeat, and every `product_id` exists in `Product`.

Report every product whose sales **all** fall in the first quarter of 2019, that is, every `sale_date` is between `2019-01-01` and `2019-03-31`, both ends included. A product needs at least one sale to be reported; a product that was never sold is left out. Each qualifying product appears once.

Return the columns `product_id` and `product_name`, in any order.
reference:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM Product AS p
JOIN Sales AS s
  ON s.product_id = p.product_id
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name
HAVING MIN(s.sale_date) >= '2019-01-01'
  AND MAX(s.sale_date) <= '2019-03-31';
brute:
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM Product AS p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Sales AS s WHERE s.product_id = p.product_id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM Sales AS s
    WHERE s.product_id = p.product_id
      AND (s.sale_date < '2019-01-01' OR s.sale_date > '2019-03-31')
  )
notes:
## Intuition

"Sold only in the quarter" means two things at once: the product has at least one sale, and none of its sales lie outside 2019-01-01 to 2019-03-31. Grouping the sales by product reduces each product's dates to a range: if its **earliest** sale is on or after January 1 and its **latest** sale is on or before March 31, every sale in between is inside the quarter too.

## Approach

1. Join `Product` (alias `p`) to `Sales` (alias `s`) on `product_id`. The inner join drops products that were never sold.
2. `GROUP BY` the product, so each product becomes one row however many sales it had (duplicates included).
3. `HAVING` keeps a group only when `MIN(s.sale_date)` is at least `2019-01-01` and `MAX(s.sale_date)` is at most `2019-03-31`.

## Example 1, step by step

| product | sale dates | MIN | MAX | kept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 S8 | 2019-01-21 | 2019-01-21 | 2019-01-21 | yes |
| 2 G4 | 2019-02-17, 2019-06-02 | 2019-02-17 | 2019-06-02 | no |
| 3 iPhone | 2019-05-13 | 2019-05-13 | 2019-05-13 | no |

Only `(1, S8)` remains.

## Complexity

- Time: O(P + S) to join and group P products with S sales using hashing (O(S log S) if the engine sorts to group).
- Space: O(P) for one group per product.

## Pitfalls

- Filtering with `WHERE sale_date BETWEEN ...` before grouping hides the out-of-quarter sales instead of disqualifying the product, so G4 would wrongly appear.
- `product_id NOT IN (products sold outside the quarter)` alone also reports products with no sales at all.
- Checking only `MONTH(sale_date) <= 3` forgets the year: a sale in February 2020 is not in the 2019 quarter.
- Without grouping (or `DISTINCT`), a product with several qualifying sales is reported several times.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `p` | `Product`, supplies the id and name |
| `s` | `Sales`, one row per sale of the product |
| `MIN(s.sale_date)` | the product's first sale date |
| `MAX(s.sale_date)` | the product's last sale date |

narration.1: Output each qualifying product's id and name.
narration.3: An inner join keeps only products that have at least one sale.
narration.4: Each sale is matched to its product by product_id.
narration.5: Grouping by product collapses all of its sales, duplicates included, into one row.
narration.6: The earliest sale must not be before the quarter starts.
narration.7: The latest sale must not be after the quarter ends, so every sale lies inside it.
